articles.title: Updated Top 25 WNBA Player Rankings Ahead of 2026 Playoffs
articles.summary: With just one week left in the WNBA regular season, it's time for one final update to our top 25 player rankings ahead of the playoffs.
articles.body:
With just one week left in the WNBA regular season, it's time for one final update to our top 25 player rankings ahead of the playoffs.

These rankings are based entirely on what players have done this season. Availability matters, too. Players who have missed significant time and played fewer than 50 percent of their team's games won't be ranked, which leaves players like Kelsey Plum and Napheesa Collier out of consideration.

We also place a lot of value on two-way impact. Offensive production matters, but so does what a player brings defensively and how they contribute to winning basketball. Though, of course, if you're having a historic season on one side of the ball, you can make up for this.

With that said, let's get into the final rankings.

At just 22 years old, Leite has already done something no other player in league history has. She's generating 22.4 points per game out of pick-and-roll, according to Synergy Sports.

Leite is almost impossible to keep in front of ball screens. She gets two feet in the paint at-will, whether it's blowing by her defender for an easy layup, drawing fouls at a historic rate or forcing the defense to help and opening up passing windows. Her assist rate also jumped from 22.4 percent to 42.5 percent this season.

The next step for Leite is building on the shooting improvements she made this year by increasing her 3-point volume—specifically off the catch. It would also be nice if she could make some strides defensively, even if she's unlikely to ever be a positive on that end.

Iriafen is the third-best player on a team that is eight games over .500 in just her second season, and she deserves a ton of credit for that. Iriafen dominates on the glass, runs the floor hard, scores efficiently around the rim and is a very good team defender.

Before the Olympic break, Iriafen had a five-game stretch with at least 18 points and 10 rebounds—tied for the third-longest such streak in WNBA history and the longest by a player under 25 years old.

What keeps Iriafen from ranking higher is her struggles as a primary rim protector and as a shooter from almost everywhere on the floor.

A year ago, Mabrey was firmly in the low-efficiency, shot-chucker bucket in Connecticut. Now, in Toronto, she's put together the most efficient pull-up 3-point shooting season (40.4% on 4.4 attempts per game) by any player not named Kelsey Mitchell.

Toronto's season was plagued by injuries, and even when healthy, the team struggled to beat good opponents. But Mabrey has flourished under Sandy Brondello, putting together a career year as a driver, playmaker, shot creator and movement shooter.

It's been fun to watch Williams back in her natural scoring role next to Olivia Miles. Her mid-range scoring has been elite as always, while the playmaking relief allows her to really lock in on the ball defensively.

Though, Williams hasn't been quite as effective since Napheesa Collier returned, averaging just 10.9 points on 41.4 percent shooting from the field over her last 12 games. That has pushed her down a bit and out of All-WNBA consideration.

Last month, Ogwumike announced she would retire from the WNBA at the end of the season, but if she wanted to keep playing, she could continue performing at an All-Star level for a couple more years.

Ogwumike is averaging 17.2 points, 8.9 rebounds and 3.0 assists on 60 percent true shooting. She's shot over 50 percent from two in every season of her career—a feat nobody else has accomplished—while also developing into a serious shooter over the back half of her career.

Burton is the best two-way point guard in the WNBA, and it's not much of a debate. She's elite defensively, shoots threes at a solid level, draws fouls and almost always makes the right decision with the ball.

Burton is averaging 6.4 assists to just 0.8 turnovers per game since the All-Star break, including a two-game stretch against Connecticut and New York where she recorded 20 assists without a single turnover.

Citron's 3-point shooting has regressed by more than 10 percent since her rookie season, but that hasn't stopped her from improving in almost every other area.

She's an outstanding driver, reading angles incredibly well, changes speeds and uses ball pickups at perfect spots to score efficiently around the rim. Citron's also a great cutter with an innate feel for off-ball movement and high-level wing defender who has taken on more lead-guard responsibilities in the process.

Citron has nearly doubled her pick-and-roll volume, going from 5.5 pick-and-rolls per game in 2025 (0.87 points per possession) to 9.7 this season (0.96).

Jones is the best shooting center in women's basketball history. This season, she's knocking down nearly 40 percent of her threes on a career-high 4.7 attempts per game.

On top of that, there aren't many players at her size who can handle the ball like she can. Head coach Chris DeMarco has found creative ways to use Jones in inverted ball screens, and it's tough to stop.

What keeps Jones from being an All-WNBA player like she was in 2024 (and the many years prior) is her defensive decline and inconsistent effort on that end. New York's defensive rating is 3.9 points worse per 100 possessions with her on the court compared to when she's off.

It's been a disastrous season for the Phoenix Mercury, but make no mistake: Thomas is still very good at basketball. She's averaging 14.2 points, 7.7 rebounds and 8.4 assists per game on 51.2 percent shooting from the field.

However, she's taken a step back defensively and hasn't been quite as dominant as a ball-screen creator, evident by her 6.1 percent drop from 2025 in efficiency out of pick-and-roll.

There are questions to be had about Shepard's defense and impact on playoff basketball, but don't let that cloud what she's done for the Dallas Wings this season.

She's one of the most unique stars we've ever seen, with her combination of passing, rebounding, screening and open-court creation at 6'4". Shepard is the perfect offensive fit next to Paige Bueckers, allowing her to maximize her premier off-ball skill set.

Reese isn't your conventional star, but she impacts winning in so many different ways. She's the best rebounder in WNBA history, a lock for an All-Defensive team and an elite transition scorer who consistently turns defense into offense.

Is she an efficient interior scorer? No. Can she shoot? No, absolutely not. Yet, she makes everyone around her better and shows up when it matters most.

Atlanta's defense is 14.2 points better per 100 with her on the court compared to when she's off, while only being marginally worse offensively (-1.9).

Howard went back to play under Cheryl Reeve, got to run ball screens with rookie Olivia Miles and somehow discovered the Fountain of Youth.

At 35 years old, she's the best play finisher in basketball, ranking first in 2-point field goals out of pick-and-roll (72) and third as a cutter (53). Howard is also an elite defender, with versatility in ball screens and the athleticism and length to be just as impactful in help.

It might be tough for Indiana to get three All-WNBA players if they finish outside of the top three, but Boston is right there in the mix.

She went from shooting 26.2 percent from three (17 made) over her first three seasons to 40.8 percent (40 made and counting) this year. There's not much she can't do offensively now.

Boston hasn't been quite as elite defensively this year, but there's no doubt she's the most valuable defender on the Fever. Opponents shoot 6.6 percent worse at the rim with Boston on the court, compared to when she's off.

This might seem low, but it has more to do with other players leveling up their games than any decline from Gray. You're really just splitting hairs in the No. 7-13 range.

This season, Gray has posted career highs in points (19.3) and 2-point percentage (54.4%), while also being a well-above-average wing defender.

But for as good as she is as an interior scorer, her shooting hasn't been at the 2025 level. Against playoff teams, she's shooting 31.9 percent from the mid-range and 30.1 percent from three. Those numbers jump to 65.2 percent and 37.2 percent, respectively, against non-playoff teams.

Williams' developmental arc since entering the WNBA has been truly insane. She was once a defense-only specialist who was scared to take threes, and now the defense is still just as elite while she's become someone teams have to respect from beyond the arc.

Golden State has so much depth that Williams only plays 24.8 minutes per game, yet she still averages 14.3 points. If you adjust that to per-36 minutes, she's at 20.8 points, right there with Allisha Gray (21.1) and Jackie Young (21.0).

Williams over Gray in these rankings might be a hot take, but Golden State did go 3-0 in the regular-season matchups against Atlanta, with Williams outplaying Gray head-to-head.

2026 Stats: 18.1 PTS, 3.1 REB, 2.2 AST, 41.7% 3P

It's completely insane that McBride wasn't an All-Star. She's the best movement shooter in the league and a very good driver who uses her gravity as a downhill creator and cutter. On top of that, McBride should be in the All-Defense conversation.

She's on pace to become the third player in WNBA history to shoot 50 percent from two, 40 percent from three and 90 percent from the free-throw line while averaging at least 1.5 steals per game in a season, joining Napheesa Collier in 2025 and Brandy Reed in 2000.

9. Shakira Austin, C, Washington Mystics

2026 Stats: 16.9 PTS, 9.4 REB, 2.5 AST, 48.9% FG

In our last player rankings article in June, Austin was left out of our Top 25. Now, we're making the case for her to be a second-team All-WNBA player. So, what changed?

It's not like Austin was having a bad first half of the season. Washington was winning games, and she was one of their most impactful players. But the turnovers were an issue, and her efficiency was inconsistent from game to game.

Since the start of July, though, there's a real case that Austin has been the best player in the league outside of A'ja Wilson. She's averaging 19.8 points and 9.6 rebounds on 51.9 percent shooting from the field while anchoring the No. 2 defense over that 22-game stretch.

The way Austin moves and attacks downhill at her size is insane, so Washington has started to weaponize these skills as a pick-and-roll creator. Since the All-Star break, she's ran 2.3 ball screens per game for 1.22 points per possession, compared to 1.4 for 0.54 PPP prior to that.

2026 Stats: 18.9 PTS, 4.4 REB, 6.6 AST, 48.3% FG

If it weren't for Jackie Young's slow start over her first seven games (10.1 points on under 35 percent shooting), she'd be averaging 20.8 points and 6.8 assists on 59 percent shooting from two and 41.4 percent from three.

The shot creation is elite, the finishing is unreal, she has the best floater in the league and her ability to create advantages as a passer is high-level, too. But the entire body of work and high-level two-way impact still matter, giving Howard (two-way impact) and Bueckers (body of work) a slight edge for us.

2026 Stats: 18.3 PTS, 3.8 REB, 3.6 AST, 41.0% FG

Howard is one of the best shooters in the league, an unquestioned top-two wing defender in the world, an improved 2-point scorer and almost never turns the ball over.

Here's the list of players in WNBA history to post at least a 3% steal rate, 2% block rate and shoot 35% from three on at least two attempts per game:

Tamika Catchings, four times – finished top five in MVP every season

2026 Stats: 20.5 PTS, 4.1 REB, 5.9 AST, 50.6% FG

It only took Bueckers until her second season to lead Dallas back to the postseason, thanks to her outrageous offensive impact.

She might go down as the greatest mid-range scorer in basketball history, on top of being one of the best off-ball movers and processors we've ever seen. Oh yeah, she's also taking pull-up threes now and knocking them down at a near 40 percent clip.

It's crazy, but Bueckers' biggest flaw is herself. Her passiveness at times is puzzling, and her willingness to get to the rim has gotten worse, if anything. As a rookie, 18.4% of her shots in the half court came at the rim—that number is down to just 12.7% in 2026. We've also seen more fouls than ever before in the WNBA, yet Bueckers' free-throw rate has only increased by 5 percent.

2026 Stats: 22.5 PTS, 3.9 REB, 8.4 AST, 45.6% FG

Clark is the engine behind the greatest offensive team in WNBA history.

She sees everything as a pick-and-roll and transition creator, and her gravity allows her to create more efficient looks for her teammates than anyone else in the league. And now, she's added a legitimate floater and the pull-up jumper has started to fall consistently, too.

Since the start of July, Clark is shooting 49.1 percent on pull-up twos (28-57) and 43.6 percent on pull-up threes (48-110).

When Clark has the pull-up three going, teams have to sell out even harder on her jumpers. Well, but she's got the in-between game going, too, and the finishing is elite. When all of that is on, there's no answer and that's been the case for a couple months.

2026 Stats: 25.0 PTS, 1.7 REB, 2.8 AST, 51.3% FG

Kelsey Mitchell is the best small-guard scorer in basketball history (under 5'9" in the WNBA and 6'2" in the NBA). There's an argument for Kelsey Plum, Jalen Brunson, Allen Iverson and 2017 Isaiah Thomas, but none of those players can score from everywhere and in every play type quite like Mitchell.

Here's the full picture of her 2026 season:

57.1% effective field-goal percentage out of PnR — No. 2 in the league

I see the argument for Clark over Mitchell because of her impact in more areas, but Mitchell has been the better player in the biggest games. Her 62.7 percent true-shooting is nearly 10 percentage points higher than Clark against playoff teams.

3. Breanna Stewart, PF, New York Liberty

2026 Stats: 20.4 PTS, 8.1 REB, 3.2 AST, 46.5% FG

Breanna Stewart was once a 37.5% 3-point shooter over a four-year stretch. Now, she's shooting 25% from three, and she's still a top-five player in the world.

That's because there are so many other ways for her to impact the game. She's an elite transition player, cutter, foul-drawer and passer who can score as both a roller and ball-handler out of ball screens.

Stewart also dominates on the glass and can defend almost any position. She's one of five players in the league averaging at least a steal and block per game.

2026 Stats: 19.7 PTS, 4.6 REB, 6.0 AST, 49.5% FG

Miles is the best player on the best team in the league… as a rookie. If A'ja Wilson weren't the greatest player of all time, Miles would probably be the second rookie to win MVP in the WNBA and the fourth to win in basketball history.

She's already the most dynamic passer and driver in the world. Miles can make any pass from virtually any spot on the court, while getting to the rim whenever she wants and finishing with either hand better than any guard in the league.

She's not always guarded like the 40 percent 3-point shooter she is, but she's making defenses pay when they go under screens. Over her last 19 games, Miles is shooting 42.2 percent from three on 5.0 attempts per game, compared to 32.8 percent on 3.4 attempts over her first 19.

Just keep in mind, this is the worst she's going to be.

2026 Stats: 26.0 PTS, 9.4 REB, 3.2 AST, 52.3% FG

Wilson is the best player in the WNBA, and there's a larger gap between her and the field than any other major sports league in the United States (and maybe the world).

Wilson is averaging 26.0 points, 9.4 rebounds, 3.2 assists and 2.0 blocks on 54.3 percent shooting from two and 39.8 percent from three.

There's nothing she can't do. Wilson can score on the interior, create her own shot in the mid-range, hit catch-and-shoot jumpers, pass, rebound and defend at a high level.

Las Vegas is 25.9 points better per 100 possessions with Wilson on the court than when she's off. That's the difference between the best team in the league when she plays and the worst team when she sits.

articles.title: LeBron James’ son Bronny James gets stern warning as his fight for a playing spot looms
articles.summary: NBA News: Bronny James is staring down the most pressure-packed stretch of his short NBA career, and the warnings keep piling up. The Los Angeles Lakers guarant.
articles.body: Bronny James is staring down the most pressure-packed stretch of his short NBA career, and the warnings keep piling up. The Los Angeles Lakers guaranteed his salary for this season, but that security comes with a catch: earn a real role, or watch the roster math turn against him fast.As the training camp is closing in, the message coming out of the Lakers' orbit is pretty clear. James has flashed the tools people keep pointing to, yet none of that matters if he can't turn brief bursts into something consistent.Bronny James gets stern warning ahead of new NBA seasonSince his father, LeBron James, left Los Angeles this summer, Bronny has been a subject of discussion. Every scoreless stretch gets picked apart, every shooting slump becomes a storyline, and now comes pointed calls for him to reshape his entire game plan.Writing for LakeShowLife.com, Tyler Watts laid out what the Lakers actually need from James this year, holding up Oklahoma City's Cason Wallace as the blueprint.“The Los Angeles Lakers showed faith in Bronny James this summer, but they need him to crack the rotation to stick long-term,” Watts wrote.Wallace forged his role through tenacious perimeter defense, smart spacing and timely playmaking rather than shot creation, and Watts believes James has to copy that formula to survive final cuts.“Bronny isn’t going to be an on-ball creator in LA. He must embrace the role Cason Wallace has played for the Oklahoma City Thunder as an undersized guard who plays stout defense, spaces the floor, and can create offense when needed. The Lakers should feed James tape of Wallace and convince him this is his path to playing time.”James already shows pieces of that defensive foundation. He has held up guarding smaller, quicker ball handlers in G League.Head coach JJ Redick pointed to Indiana's TJ McConnell and Miami's Davion Mitchell last year as the type of player James should study, and Watts figures that advice still holds now. If James turns into a connector guard who guards point of attack and complements Luka Doncic or Austin Reaves in the backcourt, extra playing time tends to follow on its own.Bronny James has to fight for playing spotTurns out James isn't the only one sweating roster decisions this fall. The Lakers loaded up on guards over the offseason, and three names are now competing for one open spot: Dalton Knecht, Jaden Hardy and James himself.Hardy arrived through the Deandre Ayton trade and owns a career 38.6% clip from three, though his defense and playmaking still trail what a rotation piece needs to offer. Knecht has slid the other direction since his rookie season, watching his minutes and shooting numbers shrink each year, and the front office has to settle his team option before Halloween.Of the three, James still looks like the safest bet to stick. The Lakers guaranteed his salary early in the offseason, a move made just before LeBron left the franchise, and that alone signals some patience from the front office. His production improved too. Across 42 games in 2025, the guard averaged 2.9 points, 1.2 assists and 0.5 rebounds in 8.9 minutes a night, modest numbers on paper, but his three-point shooting climbed from 28.1% to 38.6%, real growth from a player once written off as a name-only draft pick.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: Kawhi Leonard Isn't 'Championship Chasing,' Reflects on Trade to Raptors from Clippers in New Video
articles.summary: Now that he is officially back with the Toronto Raptors, Kawhi Leonard has reflected on the process that led to his return to the team he won a championship with during the 2018-19 season.
articles.body:
Now that he is officially back with the Toronto Raptors, Kawhi Leonard has reflected on the process that led to his return to the team he won a championship with during the 2018-19 season.

In a new video released by the Raptors (starts at 4:00 mark), Leonard explains he's not "championship chasing" at this latter stage of his career.

"I'm not really championship chasing, trying to find the best team that can win," he said. "You know, I didn't want to put on a thousand jerseys. The city took a liking to my family. I took a liking to the city. Really enjoyed it. My son was born here, and you know, he's been asking me forever when he's gonna come back. So, now he's back, and he's able to see it rather than me tell him the great stories that happened."

Landing Spots for Top 5 Unsigned NBA Free Agents 🏀

Even though Leonard isn't only pursuing titles, it's hard not to look at what his addition means for the Raptors in their quest to get back to being a championship contender in the Eastern Conference.

Toronto improved by 16 wins from 2024-25 to 2025-26, finishing with a 46-36 record last season. It was the team's most victories in a season since 2019-20.

Leading the way for that improvement was Scottie Barnes, who made the All-Star team for the second time in three years and finished fifth in Defensive Player of the Year voting.

It's not a surprise at one point in the video, Leonard said the Raptors are "his team" referencing Barnes and he wants to do "whatever it takes to help" in whatever ways he can.

A healthy Leonard can be a game-changer for the Raptors and the Eastern Conference. He is coming off one of the best regular-season performances of his career, averaging 27.9 points on 50.5 percent shooting, 6.4 rebounds and 3.6 assists per game in 2025-26.

The most encouraging stat from Leonard last season was 65 games played, his second-most since 2017-18. If the Raptors get that many games from him in 2026-27, they have the pieces to challenge the top-tier teams in the East like the New York Knicks, Philadelphia 76ers and Boston Celtics.

articles.title: La reivindicación de Causeur: "El Real Madrid debería retirar los números de algunas leyendas"
articles.standfirst: El exjugador es partidario de que el club cuelgue las camisetas de Rudy Fernández, Felipe Reyes y Sergio Llull
articles.summary: El exjugador es partidario de que el club cuelgue las camisetas de Rudy Fernández, Felipe Reyes y Sergio Llull
articles.body: Fabien Causeur ha vuelto a abrir en las redes sociales un debate recurrente entre los aficionados del Real Madrid: la retirada de dorsales que han vestido jugadores míticos de la sección. El club blanco, pese a las leyendas que han vestido esa camiseta, sólo tiene colgada del techo la de Fernando Martín, fallecido en accidente de tráfico en 1989. El exjugador francés ha escrito en sus redes sociales: "Creo que el Real Madrid debería retirar los números de algunas leyendas. O por lo menos no dejar a otro jugador usar algunos números. No me puedo imaginar a alguien llevar el 23 después de Sergi [Llull], el 9 de Felipe [Reyes] o el 5 de Rudy [Fernández]. Hablo por los que más me han impactado". Después de siete temporadas en el club blanco, Causeur parece una voz autorizada para hablar del asunto. Ganó 14 títulos con dos Euroligas, cuatro Ligas Endesa, dos Copas del Rey y seis Supercopas Endesa y salió el equipo en 2024 después de dejar una profunda huella en los aficionados y en el seno del equipo. Lo cierto es que han sido tantos los jugadores ilustres que han pasado por el Madrid que habría que retirar numerosos dorsales. el 4 de Wayne Brabender, el 5 de Rudy Fernández y Vicente Ramos, el 6 de Fernando Romay, el 9 de Felipe Reyes, el 11 de Juan Antonio Corbalán y Arvydas Sabonis, el 12 de Rafa Rullán, el 13 de Clifford Luyk y Sergio Rodríguez, el 15 de Mirza Delibasic... Pese a la reclamación de un ídolo reciente como es Causeur, no parece que el Madrid vaya a cambiar una filosofía que se mantiene en el tiempo y cuya única excepción es la del malogrado Fernando Martín.

articles.title: La selección femenina sube al tercer puesto del ránking FIBA tras el bronce en el Mundial
articles.standfirst: España asciende tres puestos y se queda sólo por detrás de Estados Unidos y Francia, finalistas en el torneo
articles.summary: España asciende tres puestos y se queda sólo por detrás de Estados Unidos y Francia, finalistas en el torneo
articles.body: Después del Mundial, FIBA ha actualizado el ránking femenino de selecciones y, tras conseguir la medalla de bronce, España ha ascendido tres puestos para encaramarse a la tercera plaza. Por delante sólo tiene a Estados Unidos y Francia, los dos equipos que disputaron la final del campeonato. En su camino hacia el Top 3, la selección española ha superado a Australia, China y Bélgica, que le antecedían en la última clasificación. Ahora la posición de España parece sólida pues supera a Alemania, cuarta por más de 100 puntos mientras que está a unos 50 de la segunda posición de Francia. La tercera plaza es la mejor posición de España en el ránking FIBA femenino desde febrero de 2022, cuando llegó a estar segunda sólo por detrás de la inalcanzable Estados Unidos. Con la generación actual y las jóvenes que cada verano conquistan medallas en categorías de formación, viene una época esperanzadora para la selección femenina, que podría asentarle en ese Top 3 mundial.
